claim: Wolfe plants each clue exactly once and refuses to repeat it, on the principle that a clue told five times is written for someone dumber than the reader.
source: Jordan 1992 interview (Shadows of the New Sun)
quote: I try not to leave a clue more than once

verdict.trueWording: 'I try not to leave a clue more than once ... if you tell me five times then I feel that you are writing for somebody that is a lot dumber than I am' (p.121).
verdict.note: Quote verbatim on p.121. Both limbs on the page; he also says 'So I try and leave my clues once.' Only softening: he says 'I try not to', a shade less absolute than the claim's 'refuses'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "refuses to repeat it" — the note says Wolfe's own words are the hedged "I try not to", "a shade less absolute than the claim's 'refuses'".

feature: style suited to the story; journalistic third person
claim: He writes each book in the style its story calls for; the third-person Long Sun therefore came out as plain, journalistic prose rather than the stylized first-person of the Severian books.
quote: pretty much straightforward journalistic prose

verdict.trueWording: 'It isn't a highly very stylized series at all, largely because it is third person. I basically feel that you should write the story in the style that corresponds to the story that you have to tell... but it comes out as a pretty much straightforward journalistic prose' (p.103).
verdict.note: Quote verbatim and the first two limbs (style follows story; third-person Long Sun as plain journalistic prose) are explicit. The contrast with Severian is not: the phrase 'first person' appears nowhere in the 31-page interview (grepped), and this passage names no book as the stylized counter-example - Jordan only asks whether it will be in 'any of the particular styles you have used before'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the contrast term 'the stylized first-person of the Severian books' - the interview never says 'first person' anywhere, and does not name Severian's style as the thing Long Sun differs from

claim: The Soldier books are built to show the problems of a genuinely good man who cannot remember, which Wolfe maps onto a decent society that has no awareness of its history.
quote: a genuinely good man who can't remember

verdict.trueWording: 'The book really is intended to show the problems faced by a genuinely good man who can't remember. Because it seems to me that is the problem of our society... our society has no memory because it has no awareness of history.' (p.118)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim and the society mapping explicit ('We have a genuinely good society... quite decent individuals'; 'this America blundering around on the world stage more or less as Latro does'). Page says singular 'The book' (Soldier of Arete under discussion) where the claim says 'The Soldier books'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "The Soldier books" (plural) — the note says the page says singular "The book", with Soldier of Arete the volume under discussion.

claim: Asked whether he invented any words, Wolfe answers that some odd words in the New Sun are typos, warning readers against treating every oddity as a clue.
quote: some of them are typos

verdict.trueWording: 'You didn't make up any words?' - 'No, but some of them are typos. Ushas is not one of them though.' (p.128)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim, and the first two limbs are exact: he is asked whether he invented words and answers that some of the odd Severian words are typos. He draws no lesson from it and says nothing about clues; the reader-warning is the researcher's gloss, not on the page.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'warning readers against treating every oddity as a clue' - Wolfe issues no warning and never mentions clues here; he only answers the Ushas question and moves on to Qabbalistic sources

claim: For the New Sun he refused Tars-Tarkas-style invented names and used archaic names and terms in contexts where the reader can work out what is meant.
quote: not coining Tars Tarkas type names

verdict.trueWording: "I started out with the idea of not coining Tars Tarkas type names"
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the attribution to The Book of the New Sun specifically - the page says only 'I felt in this book I am not going to do that', answering a question about 'both of the Sun works'; neither Wolfe nor the interviewer names the New Sun in this exchange
verdict.note: Raw PDF p.173-174. Quote verbatim. The method limb is fully supported: 'What's right is using archaic names and archaic terms for things in connections in which it will be clear to the reader what is meant.' Only the book attribution is unsupported by this page.

feature: narrator may comment; author may not
claim: First person puts the reader inside the story and lets the narrator comment on actions, whereas authorial comment is usually ruinously bad.
quote: it's usually ruinously bad

verdict.trueWording: "If the author comments from his viewpoint, it's usually ruinously bad."
verdict.note: Clarkesworld 2015 raw (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim. Page: 'When you have a first person narrator, you are much more into the story. Also, the first person narrator can comment from his viewpoint on actions.' Note the page's 'you are much more into the story' is the writer's vantage as much as the reader's; the claim's 'puts the reader inside the story' is a mild gloss but consistent with the answer's contrast to third person distance.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "puts the reader inside the story" — the note says the page's "you are much more into the story" is the writer's vantage as much as the reader's, and calls the claim's phrasing "a mild gloss".

feature: reader sees self in the text
claim: Off-the-wall interpretations no longer surprise him because readers look into the story and see themselves.
quote: what they are seeing is themselves

verdict.trueWording: "I've been doing this too long to be surprised"
verdict.note: Clarkesworld 2015 raw. Quote 'what they are seeing is themselves' is verbatim ('Somebody can look into the story and what they are seeing is themselves'), and the non-surprise is on the page. But the page attributes the non-surprise to long experience, not to readers seeing themselves; the two remarks sit side by side without the causal link the claim asserts.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the causal 'because' — the page gives long experience, not readers seeing themselves, as the reason he is no longer surprised

claim: Fictional villains have narrow viewpoints; a real villain never thinks he is a villain, which shapes how bad men narrate themselves.
quote: a real villain never thinks he's a villain

verdict.trueWording: "a real villain never thinks he's a villain"; fictional villains "have very narrow viewpoints"
verdict.note: Clarkesworld 2015 raw. Quote verbatim and the two villain limbs are on the page verbatim in substance. The third limb is an added gloss: the answer is about villains' viewpoints and the human condition, and says nothing about narration or how bad men narrate themselves (the word 'narrat-' appears only in the separate unreliable-narrator answer).
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'which shapes how bad men narrate themselves' — the page makes no claim about narration in the villain answer

claim: Severian began as a costume (boots, trousers, no shirt, cloak, mask, sword) from which Wolfe deduced the man, an executioner.
quote: He's an executioner.

verdict.trueWording: black boots, trousers, no shirt, black cloak, mask, big sword — "He's an executioner."
verdict.note: Black Gate 2010 raw. Quote verbatim, and the costume-first origin is fully on the page: the costuming panel, then 'Black boots... Black trousers... No shirt. Black cloak... A mask. A big sword. And I thought - who is this guy? The answer was obvious. He's an executioner.' But the page never names the character: 'Severian' occurs zero times in the interview (grep count 0); Wolfe names only 'the Urth of the New Sun series'. The identification is the verifier's inference, not the source's word.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the name 'Severian' — the page names only the New Sun series, never the character

claim: Military service teaches you to look at scenery as defensive positions, the perception behind Severian's line that war is a new geography.
quote: look at scenery from a standpoint of defensive positions

verdict.trueWording: "You learn to look at scenery from a standpoint of defensive positions"
verdict.note: Same page, WAR AND RELIGION section. The interviewer quotes Severian's passage ("War is not a new experience; it is a new world ... Even its geography is new, because it is a geography in which insignificant hills and hollows are lifted to the importance of cities") and Wolfe's whole reply is the quoted line. The claim's link between the Severian passage and the perception is by direct adjacency (reply to that quoted passage), not an explicit statement; the military framing is the section's own ("What military service does is rub off a lot of the pretense and self-deception").
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the link between the military perception and Severian's "war is a new geography" line — the note says that link is "by direct adjacency (reply to that quoted passage), not an explicit statement".

claim: A style becomes difficult only when it is not suited to what is being said; if it is the right style he likes it, if not he changes it.
quote: A style becomes difficult when it is not suited

verdict.trueWording: "I use the style suited to the story... If it isn't, I change it"
verdict.note: Same SF Site capture: "There really aren't any answers. I use the style suited to the story. If it's the right style for the story, I like it. If it isn't, I change it. A style becomes difficult when it is not suited to what is being said." Quote and both limbs verbatim. Wording note: the page says "becomes difficult when it is not suited"; the claim's "only when" is a (fair, context-consistent) tightening, not the page's word.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "only when" (the exclusivity) — the note says the page reads "becomes difficult when it is not suited" and that the claim's tightening is "not the page's word".

feature: secondary narrators reconstruct honestly but fallibly
claim: Daisy, principal writer of the Whorl chapters, strings others' accounts into plausible incidents and has deliberately falsified nothing, leaving errors to ignorance not intent.
quote: She has deliberately falsified nothing.

verdict.trueWording: "Daisy is the principal writer of the storyline back on the Whorl... She has done her best to string the incidents together and make everything plausible. She has deliberately falsified nothing."
verdict.note: Quote and the first three limbs verbatim. The last limb ('errors to ignorance not intent') is the direct entailment of the question it answers -- 'Have Hoof, Hide, Daisy, and Vadsig got major details wrong, deliberately, or out of ignorance?' -- but note that Wolfe does not concede the one alleged error: on the godling's size he replies 'he is far too large if he is structured along familiar lines, but who said he was?'
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "leaving errors to ignorance not intent" — the note says this limb is only "the direct entailment of the question it answers", and that Wolfe does not concede the one alleged error ("who said he was?").

claim: Asked how he came to write dimly-seen higher powers behind human events, Wolfe answers only 'No comment', leaving discovery to the reader.
quote: No comment.

verdict.trueWording: GW: "No comment."
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'leaving discovery to the reader' -- the page records only the two-word refusal and gives no reason for it
verdict.note: The question limb is exact: Jordan asks about 'a dimly-seen conflict or at least interaction of "higher powers" that is in part "behind" the human events' and 'how you came to think of writing this way'; the answer is 'No comment.' verbatim. But the page attaches no motive to the refusal. The nearest support is Gevers's introduction ('they will speak for themselves, or not at all'), which is the interviewer's characterisation of Wolfe generally, not Wolfe's account of this answer -- so the reader-discovery limb is the claim-writer's gloss, not the source's.

feature: paper is paper: the concrete credo
claim: Against a materialist correspondent Wolfe insists a piece of paper is a piece of paper and cheese is cheese, the animal-level knowing that living and, by implication, fiction require.
quote: It is paper. It is cheese.

verdict.trueWording: "the one thing that we really can't get along without is the realization that a piece of paper is a piece of paper... That's what you've got to do to live on the animal level." / "Knowing what it is. It is paper. It is cheese."
verdict.note: Quote verbatim; the correspondent is verbatim 'a materialist philosophy student who used to write to me', and the cheese figure is the mouse's 'I know cheese'. The fiction application is flagged by the claim itself as 'by implication' and is contextual: the materialism exchange grows out of Wolfe calling literary realism 'a dumbed-down part of reality'. The page never states the fiction consequence outright.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the fiction application ("and, by implication, fiction require") — the note says "The page never states the fiction consequence outright."

claim: He describes rationing The Fellowship to one chapter an evening while permitting himself to reread earlier chapters endlessly, the habit of the rereader he later writes for.
source: The Best Introduction to the Mountains (2001)
quote: no more than a single chapter each evening

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that this rationing is 'the habit of the rereader he later writes for' - the essay says nothing about Wolfe's own writing, his readers, or rereading his own books
verdict.trueWording: forcing myself to read no more than a single chapter each evening
verdict.note: Quote verbatim, and the rationing limbs are fully supported: the book is The Fellowship of the Ring, and 'The catch, my out, the stratagem by which I escaped the bonds of my own law, was that I could read that chapter as many times as I wished; and that I could also return to the chapter I had read the night before... There were evenings on which I reread the entire book up the point -- The Council of Elrond, let us say -- at which I had forced myself to stop.' Only the closing gloss tying the habit to his own later authorship is absent from the page.

feature: etymology inside and outside the story
claim: Tolkien's reply to Wolfe's fan letter distinguishes a word's etymology within the story from the author's source for it, a distinction Wolfe's own Latinate diction depends on.
source: The Best Introduction to the Mountains (2001)
quote: two sides

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that this is 'a distinction Wolfe's own Latinate diction depends on' - the essay never discusses Wolfe's diction or vocabulary
verdict.trueWording: The etymology of words and names in my story has two sides.
verdict.note: The Tolkien letter is reproduced in full on the page, dated 7th November 1966 and addressed 'Dear Mr Wolfe', after Wolfe writes 'ten years later I wrote J. R. R. Tolkien a fan letter. He answered it'. The distinction limb is exact: '(1) their etymology within the story; and (2) the sources from which I, as an author, derive them.' 'two sides' appears word for word. Only the trailing claim about Wolfe's own diction is unsupported.

claim: Rule 8 asserts the author was there and knows whose reflection they saw in the mirror, i.e. the withheld fact is known and recoverable.
source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
quote: He knows whose reflection they saw in the mirror

verdict.trueWording: He was there. He saw it happen. He knows whose reflection they saw in the mirror that night.
verdict.note: Rule 8 exact, quote verbatim as a prefix. The 'known' limb is rule 8 itself; the 'recoverable' limb is not in rule 8 but is supported elsewhere on the same page by rule 1, 'Trust the text implicitly. The answers are in there.'
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "recoverable" as an assertion of Rule 8 — the note says that limb "is not in rule 8" and rests on rule 1 elsewhere on the page.

claim: Gaiman reports Wolfe solving a ninety-year-old murder from a press clipping (the matches by the railway tracks), evidence of the engineer's mind behind the clue-planting.
source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe / journal
quote: He has an engineer's mind

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the anecdote is 'evidence of the engineer's mind behind the clue-planting' - the post never connects it to clue-planting or any technique in Wolfe's fiction (the clues in the anecdote are the police's, in a real murder case)
verdict.trueWording: He has an engineer's mind that takes things apart to see how they work and then puts them back together.
verdict.note: Fetched the journal URL itself (HTTP 200, live host). Quote verbatim, and every factual limb is on the page: 'I once read him an account of a baffling murder, committed ninety years ago... proceeded off-handedly to offer a simple and likely explanation', plus the closing parenthesis '(It was the matches on the ground, by the railway tracks, that Gene pointed to, in the old press clipping murder case, that cracked it; but of course by then the tramp was ninety years dead...)'. The post also identifies these as the first two paragraphs of the How to Read Gene Wolfe essay. Only the clue-planting gloss is the researcher's inference.

claim: Clute names the structure shared by the major works 'recursive retrospect': a narrator looking back on events whose meaning loops back on the telling.
quote: recursive retrospect

verdict.trueWording: it is a structure of unreliable Recursive retrospect ... for almost all his major book-length texts
verdict.note: The naming limb is verbatim (capital R, 'Recursive' being an SFE cross-reference): 'it is a structure of unreliable Recursive retrospect, as noted above, that Wolfe has employed for almost all his major book-length texts.' The page never glosses what recursive retrospect means; its only nearby context is that each novel is 'presented as a manuscript written down and presented to us by the protagonist of the tale, or a figure whose relationship to the protagonist is intimate'. The claim also drops 'unreliable', which is part of Clute's phrase. Grep of the whole raw page finds no second occurrence of 'retrospect' in this sense.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the gloss 'a narrator looking back on events whose meaning loops back on the telling' - the page offers no definition of the term

claim: Wolfe's reticences of presentation make the work very nearly opaque, combining the utterly present and the implacably remote.
quote: taxing reticences of presentation

verdict.trueWording: reticences ... make his work very nearly opaque TO THE SIMPLISTIC DISCOURSE-CRITICISM
verdict.note: Quote 'taxing reticences of presentation' is verbatim: 'Unfortunately the taxing reticences of presentation that monitor access to his core meanings make his work very nearly opaque to the simplistic discourse-criticism whose dominant position in sf academic work may only now be fading.' Clute's point is that a school of criticism cannot read him, not that the work is opaque per se. Separately, 'utterly present and implacably remote' IS on the page but in a different paragraph and attached to a different subject: 'his greatest texts are Modernist in a central understanding of the term: they are at one and the same time utterly present and implacably remote' - a statement about his Modernism, not about the reticences. The claim welds two independent sentences into one causal claim.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'make the work very nearly opaque' unqualified - the page says opaque to the simplistic discourse-criticism dominant in sf academia, not opaque as such

claim: Peace is a childhood narrated all unknowingly from beyond the grave, its truth value unrelentingly put under the question.
quote: unrelentingly put under the question

verdict.trueWording: who tells the story of his childhood and young manhood, all unknowingly, from beyond the grave
verdict.note: The 'beyond the grave' limb is near-verbatim in the Peace paragraph: 'The protagonist of the book - who tells the story of his childhood and young manhood, all unknowingly, from beyond the grave.' The quoted phrase, however, occurs only in the preceding Fifth Head paragraph: 'a formalizing of the confessional mode whose truth value is unrelentingly put under the question', introduced by 'As with all his most important work to date' - a generalisation that arguably reaches Peace but is never applied to Peace on the page. Cross-paragraph transfer, so PARTIAL rather than VERIFIED.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'its truth value unrelentingly put under the question' as a statement about Peace - the quoted phrase sits in the Fifth Head of Cerberus paragraph

claim: The Latro books frame the scrolls through a translator who notes the narrator's limited ability to write and the haste of composition, layering unreliability.
quote: limited ability to write

verdict.trueWording: Latro writes with limited ability per the scrolls' translator
verdict.note: Raw page (aidanmoher.com, HTTP 200). Verbatim: 'he is an otherwise uneducated mercenary with limited ability to write (per the "translator" of the found scrolls) ... and who would have been writing his recollections in haste in often difficult circumstances'. The parenthetical attributes only the writing-ability limb to the translator; the haste is Gerwel's own inference. Translator-framed scrolls and layered unreliability ('Latro is unreliable on many levels') are supported.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the translator, rather than the essayist, noting the haste of composition

claim: Wolfe's density comes from what he leaves out rather than elaborate description; suggestion through omission gives the prose its depth.
quote: what Wolfe's leaves out that gives it its depth

verdict.trueWording: Wolfe's prose is not dense; omission gives it its depth
verdict.note: Raw page (murrayewing.co.uk, HTTP 200). Verbatim: "It's what Wolfe's leaves out that gives it its depth." But the preceding sentences read 'I don't think Wolfe's prose is particularly dense. In fact, it's quite cut back and simplified'. The page attributes DEPTH, not density, to omission, and the 'rather than elaborate description' limb is supported ('cut back and simplified').
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the prose has density - the page explicitly denies Wolfe's prose is particularly dense

claim: Wolfe's narrators often know little, placing them in the reader's position; 'Tracking Song' opens by telling its narrator he knows nothing.
quote: You know nothing.

verdict.trueWording: 'The key to Wolfe's narrators ... is this passage from Tracking Song'
verdict.note: Raw page (murrayewing.co.uk). 'You know nothing.' is verbatim, as the first words of a block quotation introduced only as 'this passage from "Tracking Song"'. The knowing-little limb is fully supported: they're 'unreliable' mainly because they know so little' and amnesiac narrators are 'putting them in exactly the same position as the reader'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the passage OPENS 'Tracking Song' and is addressed to its narrator - the page gives it no position in the story and names no addressee

feature: interpolated tales comment on the frame
claim: The embedded tales comment in various ways on the events Weer narrates, and the reader must decide which ones do.
quote: comment in various ways on the events

verdict.trueWording: Interpolated tales comment on events Weer narrates and people he knew
verdict.note: Raw page (blog.ayjay.org). Verbatim: 'The various interpolated tales in Peace comment in various ways on the events that Weer narrates and the people that he knew.' Jacobs then supplies his own identifications ('one story about a princess and her suitors clearly mirrors Aunt Olivia'; a tale 'I think is meant to describe to Weer his own situation') without saying the reader must decide. The nearest reader-task line, 'we are left to draw inferences', is about Weer's unfinished stories, not about which tales comment.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the reader must decide WHICH tales comment on the frame - the page asserts no such reader task and instead states its own examples

feature: lie in dialogue, not in narration
claim: Wolfe's characters will lie in dialogue but not in narration, so narrative statements can be trusted while speech cannot.
quote: characters will lie in dialogue but not in narration

verdict.trueWording: Key rule: characters lie in dialogue but not in narration
verdict.note: Raw page (the-solute.com, HTTP 200). The rule is verbatim (capitalised on the page): '(Key rules: Characters will lie in dialogue but not in narration.)'. The page supports only the narrower point that the narration does not fabricate - 'he is not making up events which did not happen, though his perspective is heavily biased' - and wallflower's method is to check 'if he's being honest about the what and the why', i.e. narration is not to be trusted wholesale.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that narrative statements can therefore be TRUSTED - the same page says 'when a Wolfe narrator lies to you or tricks you' and calls Weer's narration 'essentially utter manipulation', biased and evasive

claim: Weer prides himself on remembering everything yet cannot remember the librarian's name, a self-contradiction the text leaves standing.
quote: I who pride myself upon remembering everything

verdict.trueWording: pride belongs to the old narrator, not young Weer
verdict.note: Quote is verbatim and the first two limbs hold: 'a librarian—a woman whose name Weer can't remember, something that upsets him very much, because, as he himself claims, “I who pride myself upon remembering everything.”' But the page does not call this a self-contradiction left standing — it immediately offers a reconciliation: 'This total capacity for remembrance, of course, does not belong to the young Weer, but to the old man, the narrator himself.' Nearest general support is a separate line: 'all his narrators are unreliable.'
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'a self-contradiction the text leaves standing' — the page glosses the tension rather than leaving it unresolved

claim: Latro's judgments are sound; it is his perceptions and memory that cannot be trusted, unlike Severian who may claim sudden fear or Weer who may not bury the thief.
quote: It is not Latro who can't be trusted

verdict.trueWording: "It is not Latro who can't be trusted, it is his perceptions of the world."
verdict.note: Aramini, Ultan's Library interview (Q on why Latro was chosen as narrator). Raw page reached via live URL, HTTP 200. Quote is word for word. Every limb present: "Latro is the one who will almost invariably act according to sound moral judgments"; "Severian might jump in to save a child, or he might stand back and claim that he was suddenly overcome with fear"; "Weer might or might not bury someone who tried to steal from him." One wording nuance: Aramini names "his perceptions of the world", not "perceptions and memory"; memory enters only as "He is unreliable only insofar as people try to use his lack of memory against him."
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "and memory" — the note says Aramini names "his perceptions of the world", not "perceptions and memory".

claim: Wolfe's endings are often melancholy and inconclusive; Soldier of the Mist ends with the amnesiac finding a man who knows him only as he dies.
quote: his endings are often melancholy

verdict.unsupportedLimb: "and inconclusive" as a general property of Wolfe's endings
verdict.trueWording: "Except for a few very notable exceptions, his endings are often melancholy"
verdict.note: Same raw page. The melancholy limb is verbatim but carries a qualifier the claim drops ("Except for a few very notable exceptions"). The Soldier of the Mist limb is fully supported: "our amnesiac narrator finally locates someone who knows him, dying there on the battlefield, and he can only give comfort" (Aramini calls it "the first novel"). Inconclusiveness is asserted on the page only of one book - Soldier of Sidon's ending is "even less conclusive than Soldier of Arete" - and Aramini elsewhere pushes the other way: "Wolfe is a modernist who merely pretends to create inconclusive subjectivity; his elided structures point at 'correct' conclusions that are often implied." Generalising "inconclusive" across Wolfe's endings is not what the page says.

claim: The stories are engineered so that seemingly inconsequential details have consequences later; every tale should be read as a mystery.
quote: seemingly inconsequential details will have consequences later on

verdict.unsupportedLimb: "every tale should be read as a mystery" - the page says virtually every tale from the '70s on
verdict.trueWording: "Virtually every tale of his from the '70s-on should be read in that fashion"
verdict.note: DMR Books, Deuce Richardson, 10 May 2019; raw page reached live, HTTP 200. First limb verbatim: "His stories are 'engineered,' in that seemingly inconsequential details will have consequences later on." The mystery limb is over-generalised twice over: the page limits it to "Virtually every tale of his from the '70s-on" and immediately qualifies "though the mystery in each is usually not of the 'whodunit?' type."

claim: Wolfe acknowledges homages (Borges, M. R. James, Crowley) and jokes that his parodic streak is about five and a half feet deep.
quote: about five and half feet

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that Wolfe acknowledges the Borges and Crowley homages - those are the interviewer's attributions, and Wolfe answers only on M. R. James
verdict.trueWording: "I'd say that the depth of my parodic streak is about five and half feet."
verdict.note: SF Site, "A Magus Of Many Suns: An Interview With Gene Wolfe", Nick Gevers, January 2002, via the Wayback capture in the URL (HTTP 200, raw HTML). The joke is verbatim - and note the page reads "five and half feet", without the "a" the claim's paraphrase inserts. The homage limb is misattributed: it is Gevers who writes "some obvious (Borges in 'Useful Phrases') but others more fugitively so (John Crowley in 'The Haunted Boardinghouse', M. R. James in 'One-Two-Three For Me')". Wolfe's entire reply on that point is "I'm amazed that you saw M. R. James in 'One-Two-Three For Me.' You're very perceptive." - and an editorial insert adds that even that was pointed out by someone else. Wolfe acknowledges no Borges or Crowley homage on this page.

claim: Gerlach argues that the reader of The Book of the Long Sun comes to occupy its city as its inhabitants do, rather than being given an explanatory overview of it.
source: John Gerlach, 'The Rhetoric of an Impossible Object: Gods, Chems, and Science Fantasy in Gene Wolfe's Book of the Long Sun', Extrapolation vol. 40 no. 2 (1999), Kent State University Press
quote: we begin to inhabit much as the characters do
routeHint: gwern.net raw PDF, browser UA, macOS Quartz text layer

verdict.trueWording: "the world we're immersed in is one we begin to inhabit much as the characters do"
verdict.note: Gerlach 1999, printed p. 155; PDF fetched as binary from gwern.net (HTTP 200, 148,965 bytes) and text-extracted. Quote verbatim. The contrastive limb is supported by the same paragraph and the one before it: "clues are so sparse the reader will focus elsewhere" and "only occasionally is a clue given to invoke again the issue of who the gods are or where this world is" - i.e. no explanatory overview. One paraphrase drift worth recording: Gerlach writes "world"/"whorl", not "city", though his supporting detail is civic ("recurring street names").
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "its city" — the note says Gerlach writes "world"/"whorl", not "city".

claim: Gerlach notes that Wolfe estranges his setting by giving ordinary English words unfamiliar in-world applications rather than by coining new ones.
quote: familiar with are applied in unusual, usually comical ways

verdict.unsupportedLimb: "rather than by coining new ones" - the same article cites Wolfe's coinages
verdict.trueWording: "Words we're familiar with are applied in unusual, usually comical ways"
verdict.note: Gerlach 1999, sentence spanning printed pp. 154-155, same extracted PDF; quote verbatim and the page cite is right. The repurposing limb is exactly Gerlach's ("'Mainframe' seems to be the place you go when you die"). But the exclusive limb is not on the page and is cut against by it: Gerlach discusses coined terms directly - "Terms like 'shadeup' and 'shadedown' are different, too" - and uses "whorl", "needler", "manteions", "chems" and "taluses" as the article's own vocabulary. Wolfe estranges by both routes here, not by repurposing instead of coining.

claim: Gerlach shows that the in-text dramatis personae preface bound into each volume of The Book of the Long Sun revises its own entry for the god called the Outsider from volume to volume, so that the record corrects itself with no narrator announcing the correction.
quote: subsequent volumes offer a truer picture

verdict.unsupportedLimb: "with no narrator announcing the correction" - Gerlach never addresses how or whether the change is announced
verdict.trueWording: "subsequent volumes offer a truer picture" of the Outsider in the prefaces
verdict.note: Gerlach 1999, printed p. 159 (cite correct), same extracted PDF. Quote verbatim, and the revision mechanism is fully evidenced: the preface "God, Persons, and Animals Mentioned in the Text" before volume 2 calls the Outsider "the minor God who enlightened Silk", the volume 3 preface "the god of the broken and the disparaged whose realm lies outside the Whorl", and volume 4 "the god of gods". What the page does not carry is the narratorial claim - Gerlach simply quotes the three successive entries and calls the shift "perhaps the most delicious irony of all"; he says nothing about a narrator announcing or failing to announce it. Second, smaller stretch: he names prefaces to volumes 2, 3 and 4 only, not one "bound into each volume".

claim: Jones reports that Wolfe's withholding in There Are Doors left her groping without guidance rather than inferring.
quote: The reader is left groping without guidance

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the groping is caused by Wolfe's *withholding*, and that it displaces inference — Jones attributes it to an incoherent, blurred dream landscape and 'oneiric confusion', and never contrasts it with reader inference
verdict.trueWording: The reader is left groping without guidance
verdict.note: Quote verbatim on printed p. 78: 'The reader is left groping without guidance in an oneiric confusion that's often barely distinguishable from malice at the printers.' But the page's diagnosis is incoherence/blur (deficient infrastructure, no coherent geography), not deliberate withholding, and Jones offers no inference-versus-groping contrast. She also writes 'The reader', not a first-person report of her own groping.

verdict.unsupportedLimb: "its narrator" — the note says Wolfe says "a man has died" and that the narrator identification is "not the page's wording".

verdict.note: Quote verbatim on printed p. 41. The 'very few readers grasp it' limb is exact. The exclusivity limb fails: immediately after the quoted sentence Wolfe adduces both the opening line ('The elm tree planted by Eleanor Bold, the judge's daughter, fell last night.') and the closing chapters, so the novel signals the fact in at least two places, not only the opening sentence.

'Resolvable rather than open' is the claim's inference from 'inevitable', consistent with the page at this point, though Wright's larger thesis still calls ambiguity 'a means of confounding interpretation'.

The error Wolfe describes is inferential, not auditory: Latro hears 'Laconic manners' accurately and draws a false etymology. Region and name (Laconia / Silent Country) are confirmed by the folk-etymology table.

But the page draws no contrast with statement: the same sentence flatly states 'we know that Silk, on the other hand, is indeed good', and the column also quotes Hoof's plain 'Father was good' and Clute's own earlier 'one of the most luminously good figures in 20th century literature'. verdict.note: Page: 'academics have notoriously tended to shun him for decades: because you cannot strip-mine Gene Wolfe for "meaning," you cannot abstract themes from stories that only make sense when it is understood how they have been told.' Quote verbatim. Clute hedges the causal link ('which may be one of the reasons') and names a second reason ('he is indeed difficult'); the claim states the reason more firmly than the page but does not misname it.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the flat causal "because" — the note says Clute hedges the link ("which may be one of the reasons") and names a second reason, so "the claim states the reason more firmly than the page".

The plot itself is apparently unremarkable.' Wright's undistinguished element is the PLOT, not the prose; the claim inverts the exception clause.

The cards-up-the-sleeve and cannot-follow-the-moves limbs are fully supported; only the 'working novelist' descriptor is not on the page.

claim: Andre-Driussi infers from a single offhand remark by a minor character that the city's name records a failure of its water treatment, and that technological decline is what poisoned the river.

But the page does not call the remark offhand, and it treats Jonas as a major interpretive figure - 'Jonas now shines for me as the man of history... he is our stand-in, our surrogate in Severian's Commonwealth' - so 'a single offhand remark by a minor character' is the claim-writer's framing, not the page's.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the source is a single offhand remark by a minor character (the page casts Jonas as a major figure and never calls the remark offhand)

claim: Andre-Driussi reconstructs from that same remark that the city had to move upstream to escape its own filth, a civic history the narrative never states outright.

verdict.trueWording: The technology fell until finally the city had to move upstream to avoid its own filth.
verdict.note: Quote is verbatim in the same section 1 paragraph, and it is plainly the critic's own inference ('it now seems crystal clear to me'). The page nowhere asserts that Wolfe's narrative never states this civic history outright, so that limb is unsupported by this source.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the narrative never states this civic history outright - the page makes no claim about what the novels do or do not state

claim: Wowra states that all the strange words in The Book of the New Sun are real English words, and that this shows how odd language can sound without invented vocabulary.

But the page says the words are 'real', never 'English'; the word 'English' does not appear anywhere on the page, and its own gloss for cherkaji is 'Persian light cavalry'.

claim: Borski reports that most of what that officer reads comes to the reader as extracts, among them taped interrogation transcripts, a field journal and a prison diary.
source: Robert Borski, review of The Fifth Head of Cerberus, Ultan's Library, 28 August 2001

verdict.note: The quoted sentence is verbatim and all three document types are on the page. The quantifier is not: the page says 'Much of what the officer examines', not 'most of what that officer reads'. The page also says 'taped interviews by various interrogators', not 'taped interrogation transcripts', and describes what the officer examines rather than how it reaches the reader.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'most' - the page says 'Much of what the officer examines'; and 'taped interrogation transcripts' for the page's 'taped interviews by various interrogators'

claim: Wolfe said the reason he rewrote that opening so many times was to establish the feeling of stagnation that governs what follows.

verdict.note: Same raw SFS capture; quote verbatim and the causal limb ('because it seemed essential to capture...') is explicit. Wording nuance, not an unsupported limb: Wolfe says the stagnation 'affects a lot of what's to follow', slightly weaker in force and scope than the claim's 'governs what follows'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "governs what follows" — the note says Wolfe's "affects a lot of what's to follow" is "slightly weaker in force and scope".

claim: Holland says the opening scene of The Fifth Head of Cerberus carries clues to a larger mystery while reading as ordinary recollection.
source: Floyd Holland, 'The Enchanting Prose of Gene Wolfe' (Substack), 2025
quote: the scene is peppered with clues to the larger story

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the scene reads as ordinary recollection — Holland never characterises it as ordinary or plain; he calls the prose dense, 'sophisticated' and 'mature', with 'acute attention to detail' and an 'intensely psychological focus', and the effect 'vivid and compelling'
verdict.note: Raw page. Quotation is verbatim. The clue-planting limb is fully supported; the contrastive limb is the researcher's addition. Holland does frame the excerpt as recollection ("the slow breakthrough of recollection") but never as ordinary or unremarkable — if anything he flags it as distinctively Wolfean ("in even more Gene Wolfe fashion").

claim: Sini says the presence Wolfe's sentences summon has contours that are not clearly defined and yet are not vague.
source: Matthew Sini, 'Great Uncle Gene', New Mythologies (Substack), 2023

Quote exact, in the paragraph on Wolfe's sentences as 'mystagogic initiation': 'The presence of "something" is brought forth, and its contours aren't always clearly defined, but it's also not vague.' Page hedges with 'always'; the claim drops it, which is the only drift.

claim: The guide asserts the information a reader needs is always present in a Wolfe text, though not where the reader expects it.

source: Michael Swanwick, 'The Wolf in the Labyrinth', F&SF 2007, reposted on Flogging Babel 2016

claim: The same essay disputes the common claim that Severian lies to the reader, holding that he does not.

One wording nuance short of an unsupported limb: Hayles writes "we CAN use that rule to derive", where the claim says the reader "must" derive — the modality is softer on the page, but the operation, the three symbols and the absence of emphasis are all stated as claimed.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: "must derive" — the note says Hayles writes "we CAN use that rule to derive", so "the modality is softer on the page".

claim: Roy C. Lackey treats a physical detail that does not belong in its setting — cart tracks on a beach — as the load-bearing evidence linking two scenes.
source: Roy C. Lackey, Urth mailing list, 10 September 2006
quote: had no business being on that beach.
page: message body, reply on the Sand Garden
routeHint: lists.urth.net dead from here (curl 000); Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/2021id_/<url>

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the cart tracks are the load-bearing evidence for the link — Lackey offers them as one corroborating detail among several ("right down to the tracks"), alongside the person to be met being Severian's future self and the concealed woman being Thecla, and he hedges the whole parallel as holding "to some extent".
verdict.trueWording: "...the Sand Garden to some extent replicated/foreshadowed what would happen months later on the beach, right down to the tracks of the two-wheeled cart, which had no business being on that beach."
verdict.note: Raw page reached via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20210416053700id_/http://lists.urth.net/pipermail/urth-urth.net/2006-September/003007.html (live host down as above). Byline and date on the page: Roy C. Lackey, rclackey at stic.net, Sun Sep 10 23:43:34 PDT 2006. The quote "had no business being on that beach." is on the page word for word, and the out-of-place-physical-detail limb (two-wheeled cart tracks on a beach) is fully supported. What the page does not support is the weight the claim assigns it: the tracks are the sharpest concrete correspondence in a list of correspondences, not stated to be the evidence the link rests on.

claim: Peter Wright relays Baird Searles's judgement that The Book of the New Sun marks a turning point of science fiction from content to style, from matter to manner.
source: Peter Wright relaying Baird Searles, Isaac Asimov's Science Fiction Magazine, May 1983, p. 167; Ultan's Library, 28 August 2002
quote: from content to style, from matter to manner
polarity: relays a sceptical framing of the book's stylistic turn

verdict.trueWording: one that perhaps marks the turning point of science fiction
verdict.note: Quotation 'from content to style, from matter to manner' is on the ultan.org.uk page verbatim, inside the same Searles block quotation, correctly footnoted. But Searles frames it as a hedged prediction about reception rather than a delivered judgement: the work will be considered a landmark, one that PERHAPS marks the turn. The claim states it flatly.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the flat 'marks a turning point' — the page hedges it as 'perhaps marks', inside a forecast of how the work will be considered
